title: High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being
book_use: Chapter 1: establishes distinction between life evaluation and emotional well-being and the influential approximately $75,000 plateau result in 2008–2009 U.S. data.

title: Experienced well-being rises with income, even above $75,000 per year
book_use: Chapter 1: experience-sampling result based on more than 1.7 million reports from 33,391 employed U.S. adults; no general plateau at the earlier threshold.

author_or_institution: Matthew A. Killingsworth; Daniel Kahneman; Barbara Mellers
title: Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved
book_use: Chapter 1: reconciles earlier findings; flattening among least-happy participants while well-being continues rising for happier groups. Preserve observational and measurement caveats.

author_or_institution: Philip Brickman; Dan Coates; Ronnie Janoff-Bulman
title: Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative?
book_use: Chapter 2: famous small-sample adaptation study; use the actual sample sizes and findings to correct the later folk claim that people simply adapt completely to fortune or disability.

author_or_institution: Erik Lindqvist; Robert Östling; David Cesarini
title: Long-Run Effects of Lottery Wealth on Psychological Well-Being
book_use: Chapter 2: randomized Swedish lottery wealth produced sustained gains in overall life satisfaction 5–22 years later, with smaller effects on happiness and mental-health measures; key counterweight to total-adaptation stories.

author_or_institution: Jonathan Gardner and Andrew J. Oswald
title: Money and Mental Wellbeing: A Longitudinal Study of Medium-Sized Lottery Wins
book_use: Chapter 2: British longitudinal evidence of improved psychological health after medium-sized lottery wins; use as another reason not to universalize the 1978 result.

author_or_institution: Andrew E. Clark and Andrew J. Oswald
title: Satisfaction and comparison income
book_use: Chapter 3: worker satisfaction relates negatively to comparison wage levels, an early empirical anchor for relative-income effects.

title: Neighbors as Negatives: Relative Earnings and Well-Being
book_use: Chapter 3: holding own income constant, higher local earnings are associated with lower reported well-being; use with identification caveats.

author_or_institution: Peter J. Kuhn; Peter Kooreman; Adriaan R. Soetevent; Arie Kapteyn
title: The Own and Social Effects of an Unexpected Income Shock: Evidence from the Dutch Postcode Lottery
book_use: Chapter 3: randomized neighborhood windfalls affected visible consumption such as cars and exterior renovation among neighbors, while six-month happiness effects were not detected; important counterexample to an overbroad comparison story.

author_or_institution: David Card; Alexandre Mas; Enrico Moretti; Emmanuel Saez
title: Inequality at Work: The Effect of Peer Salaries on Job Satisfaction
book_use: Chapter 3: below-median workers shown peer-pay information reported lower satisfaction and more job-search intent, while above-median workers did not receive symmetric gains.

author_or_institution: Leonardo Bursztyn; Bruno Ferman; Stefano Fiorin; Martin Kanz; Gautam Rao
title: Status Goods: Experimental Evidence from Platinum Credit Cards
book_use: Chapter 3: identical-benefit card variants reveal demand for visible status; social use and self-esteem intervention help isolate signaling motives.

title: The Effects of Income Transparency on Well-Being: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
book_use: Chapter 3: online public access to Norwegian tax records widened well-being gaps between richer and poorer individuals; use to show that making rank visible can change its psychological force.

title: How Much Does Your Boss Make? The Effects of Salary Comparisons
book_use: Chapter 3: information about manager pay and peer pay produced different behavioral responses, showing that comparison depends on who the reference person is and what their pay implies.

title: The role of income aspirations in individual happiness
book_use: Chapter 4: higher income aspirations are associated with lower life satisfaction holding income constant; aspirations rise with own income and average community income, supporting a moving-reference-point mechanism without implying ambition is inherently harmful.

author_or_institution: David W. Johnston and Wang-Sheng Lee
title: Extra Status and Extra Stress: Are Promotions Good for Us?
book_use: Chapter 4: promotions improve pay perceptions, job security, and job satisfaction in the short term while broader health and happiness effects are small on average; responsibilities, stress, hours, and job control also change.

title: The joy of gratifications: Promotion as a short-term boost or long-term success – The same for women and men?
book_use: Chapter 4: German longitudinal panel evidence that promotion raises job satisfaction in the short term but the effect diminishes after about one year; use as evidence for reference-point updating, not as a universal claim that promotions do not matter.

title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction
book_use: Chapter 5: reward circuitry, tolerance, compulsive drug use, and limits of treating ordinary preference as addiction by analogy.

title: American Time Use Survey
book_use: Chapter 8: empirical baseline for paid work, sleep, leisure, caregiving, and other uses of finite daily time.

title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
book_use: Chapter 9 and platform-design material: documented interface practices that can steer or manipulate user behavior; use to distinguish deliberate design from vague claims about addictive technology.

title: Problems of Monetary Management: The U.K. Experience
book_use: Chapter 11: historical source behind Goodhart's law; verify exact language and separate original claim from later formulations about metrics becoming targets.

author_or_institution: Gilles Duranton and Matthew A. Turner
title: The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities
book_use: Chapter 13: induced-demand evidence showing vehicle kilometers traveled increasing roughly proportionally with lane kilometers in U.S. interstate highways; examine limitations and policy context.

title: Engineering Statistics Handbook
book_use: Chapter 14: reliability, optimization, process capability, and diminishing-return examples; use specific sections only after verifying the exact engineering claim.
